title: The Dark Side of Leader Generosity
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article distinguishes authentic generosity from a transactional imitation of it. Real generosity, the piece argues, comes without expectation of return — leaders give because they value people, not to earn loyalty or admiration. The 'dark side' version comes with strings attached: leaders who give expecting something back, often followed quickly by a request or demand, using generosity as a manipulation tool to secure loyalty or attention. Team members, the essay notes, are quick to spot the difference, and research suggests genuinely generous leaders end up healthier and happier as a byproduct of giving without an agenda.
points: Authentic generosity comes without expectation of anything in return.
Transactional generosity — giving to get loyalty, attention, or reciprocity — is really self-interest in disguise.
Leaders with ulterior motives often follow acts of generosity with a request or demand.
Team members can quickly spot generosity that comes with strings attached.
Research suggests genuinely generous leaders are healthier and happier as a result of giving freely.
quotes: When a leader’s generosity comes with expectations, it doesn’t qualify as big-heartedness. Giving to others as a reciprocal exchange doesn’t count as generosity.
Such leaders often manipulate others through acts of kindness and giving that are over-the-top and extravagant.
Their generosity is inauthentic and comes with strings attached.
Truly generous leaders never turn to the dark side, even when they are tempted to do so. They give freely and abundantly because they value people, not to receive things in return.
As a result, research confirms they are healthier, happier, and enjoy a higher quality of life.
